title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
In this lab, I developed a C program for the STM32L432KC Microcontroller to generate musical notes using hardware timers built into the MCU. Each note was represented by a frequency in Hertz and a duration in milliseconds. TIM16 was used to control the pitch by determining when the speaker output pin should toggle, while TIM15 was used to control how long each note lasted. This separated the timing of each square-wave cycle from the timing of the overall melody.
The program used the onboard MCU-controlled GPIO pin PB7 as the digital audio output for an LM386 amplifier and an 8Ω speaker. The uploaded version contains the Für Elise song and an alternative arrangement of ‘Mary Had a Little Lamb’. The main goals were to implement memory-mapped timer drivers, relate the timer settings to the resulting pitches and durations, and evaluate the accuracy of the notes being generated.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Hardware Design
The STM32L432KC generated the square-wave input to the LM386 amplifier, which drove the 8Ω speaker. I used PB7, configured as a GPIO output, to send the square-wave signal to the amplifier and connected the microcontroller and amplifier grounds together. The amplifier was powered by a 5V supply. I also used a volume potentiometer to adjust the sound coming from the speaker. Turning it one way reduced the volume to zero, while turning it the other way made the speaker very loud. The microcontroller determined the note frequency and duration, while the amplifier drove the speaker.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
C Code Structure
The program was divided into separate files for clock configuration, GPIO control, and the two timers. Each timer had a header file containing its register definitions and function declarations, and a source file containing its initialization and playback functions. main.c combined these functions to read the musical score and generate the output.

Clock and GPIO Configuration
At the beginning of main(), setFlashLatency(4) configured the flash memory for operation at the higher clock speed. The program then called configurePLL(PLLSRC_MSI, 1, 40, 2) and selectSysclk(SW_PLL) to produce an intended system clock of 80 MHz from the 4 MHz MSI oscillator. With the bus prescalers unchanged from their reset settings, both timers also received an 80 MHz clock.
The GPIOB clock was enabled through RCC->AHB2ENR. The program then used pinMode() to configure PB7 as an output and digitalWrite() to initialize it low.


Memory-Mapped Register Access
The timer headers defined the base addresses of TIM15 and TIM16 as 0x40014000 and 0x40014400, respectively. Register structures and pointer macros allowed the program to access registers using expressions such as TIM15->PSC and TIM16->ARR. The register fields were declared volatile so that the compiler preserved accesses to hardware registers, including status flags that could change independently of the program.
The main registers used were the prescaler (PSC), auto-reload register (ARR), control register (CR1), event-generation register (EGR), and status register (SR).


TIM16: Pitch Control
TIM16 controlled the frequency of each note. TIM16_init() enabled the timer clock and set its prescaler to 79, dividing the 80 MHz input by 80 to create a 1 MHz counter clock.
TIM16_play(frequency) calculated the number of timer counts required for half of the requested square-wave period and set ARR accordingly. The calculation included rounding to the nearest integer to reduce pitch error.
Whenever TIM16 overflowed, its update flag (UIF) became set. The main loop checked this flag, cleared it, and called togglePin() to change PB7’s output state. Two toggles produced one complete square-wave cycle. Therefore, this implementation used timer-controlled software toggling rather than a hardware PWM output.


TIM15: Duration Control
TIM15 controlled how long each note played. I set PSC = 7999 to obtain a 10 kHz counter clock, so each count represented 0.1 ms. For a note duration of duration_ms, I set
\[
ARR = 10\,duration_{ms}-1.
\]
For example, a 125 ms note required 1250 timer counts, so ARR = 1249. Once TIM15 reached its overflow, the main loop stopped playing that note and moved to the next one.
Both timer playback functions generated an update event to initialize the new timing settings, cleared the resulting update flag, and enabled the counter.


Main Playback Loop
The melody was stored as a two-dimensional array containing frequency–duration pairs. For each entry, the program drove PB7 low, configured TIM16 for the requested pitch, and started TIM15 for the requested duration. It then polled both timers, toggling PB7 on TIM16 updates until TIM15 indicated that the note was complete.
A frequency of zero represented a rest. In this case, TIM16 was disabled before the frequency calculation, preventing division by zero, and PB7 remained low while TIM15 measured the pause. A duration of zero marked the end of the song. Once this entry was reached, both timers were disabled and PB7 was held low.
Für Elise was selected in the uploaded program. Mary Had a Little Lamb was included as a commented-out alternative that could use the same playback functions. I tested the playback of both of these songs, and hacing both of them stored as frequency-duration pairs allowed me to swicth songs without chnaging any timer logic.

title: Lab 4: Digital Audio
text:
Testing Methodology
I tested the system by listening to the songs through the speaker. I was able to play both Für Elise and Mary Had a Little Lamb using the same timer functions. I also tested the volume potentiometer and found that it provided a wide range of volume control, from silent at one end to very loud at the other. This let me adjust the speaker volume without changing the frequencies or durations in the code.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts and Quadrature Encoder
text:
In this lab , I developed a C program for the STM32L432KC microcontroller to read a quadrature encoder using interrupts and detect the rotational velcoity and direction of a DC motor. The encoder generates two square-wave signals (A and B) at their output channels that are 90 degrees out of phase, allowing the determination of both the position and direction of rotation.
The encoder signals were read using external interrupts on the MCU rather than polling. Both the rising and falling edges of both encoders were monitored to maximize the resolution of the position measurement. A seperate timer interrupt was used to create a one-second time window, after which the number of encoder pulses was counted and used to calculate direction and velocity. The system was designed to update the velocity and direction at 1 Hz, providing a real-time measurement of the motor’s performance.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts and Quadrature Encoder
text:
Overall C Code Structure

Clock Configuration
The STM32L432KC was configured to run at 80 MHz using the internal MSI oscillator and the PLL. This ensured that the timers and GPIOs operated correctly for accurate encoder reading and timing. The code used the MCU’s 4MHz MSI oscillator as the clock source, and the PLL was configured to multiply this frequency to achieve the desired system clock speed with the following settings: configurePLL(PLLSRC_MSI, 1, 40, 2). The PLL clock was selected as the system clock source using selectSysclk(SW_PLL). Before increasing the clock speed, the flash latency was set to 4 using to ensure proper operation at higher frequencies. This system clockw as also used for the configuration of TIM16.


Encoder GPIO Setup
The quadrature encoder’s output channels were connected to GPIO pins PA6 and PA9 on the STM32L432KC, defined in main.h as ENCODER_A_PIN and ENCODER_B_PIN. The digitalRead() helper function reads the appropriate bit from the GPIO input data register (IDR). This was used inside the encoder interrupt handler to read the current states of A and B each time an encoder edge occurred.


TIM16 and 1 Hz Configuration
TIM16 was used to create a fixed one second measurement interval. This served two purposes: it determined how long encoder pulses were accumulated before calculating velocity and controlled how often a new velocity value was printed in the terminal.
The timer was configured with a prescaler of 7999 to divide the system clock’s 80MHz speed, giving a counter frequency of 10 kHz. The ARR was then calculated to be 9999, resulting in a timer overflow every 1 second. The timer configuration in TIM16_init() sets the peripheral clock, prescaler, auto-reload value, and forces an update so the settings take effect, clears the update flag, and starts the counter.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts and Quadrature Encoder
text:
Interrupts Configuration
The design used interrupts rather than polling so that encoder edges could be recorded immediately without requiring the main loop to continuously check the input pins. The interrupt setup was written using the STM32 CMSIS register definitions. The project includes the ST device header called stm32l432xx.h, which defines the memory-mapped registers for the STM32L432KC. This allowed the peripherals to be configured without using the STM32 HAL library.
For the encoder, the SYSCFG periperal was first enabled, followed by GPIO pin PA6 being routed to EXTI6 and PA9 being routed to EXTI9. The EXTI interrupt mask register (IMR) was then set to enable interrupts for both channels. The rising and falling edge triggers were enabled in the EXTI rising trigger selection register (RTSR) and falling trigger selection register (FTSR). Finally, the NVIC was configured to enable the EXTI9_5_IRQn interrupts, which correspond to the encoder channels.
For TIM16, the timer’s update interrupt was enabled in the DIER register, and the NVIC was configured to enable the TIM16_IRQn interrupt. This allowed the main loop to be interrupted every second to calculate and print the velocity and direction of the motor. Overall, the interrupt-based structure allowed encoder edges to be recorded independently of the main loop while TIM16 maintained a consistent one-second measurement interval.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts and Quadrature Encoder
text:
Interrupts vs Manual Polling
At high motor speeds, interrupt-based code is more reliable than manual polling because the encoder can change state much faster than the main loop may be able to check the GPIO pins. To check execution time of the interrupt handlers, the code used a GPIO pin to toggle a signal at the start and end of each interrupt. This allowed the duration of the interrupt to be measured using an oscilloscope. The oscilloscope measurements showed that the interrupt handler took approximately 4 µs to execute. Since the encoder produces 120 pulses per revolution, and given that we are counting rising and falling edges of both encoder channels, we can expect around 480 detectable transitions per revolution. At the maximum recorded motor speed of approximately 10.8 rev/s at 12V, this corresponds to approximately 193 µs between consecutive encoder transitions. Since the interrupt handler requires only 4 µs, it completes well before the next expected transition, demonstrating that the interrupt-based implementation can efficiently process encoder signals while allowing the CPU to perform other tasks between interrupts.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts and Quadrature Encoder
text:
Quadrature Encoder Logic
The quadrature encoder generates two square-wave signals, A and B, that are 90 degrees out of phase. These were montitored at both the rising and falling edges of both signals to maximize the resolution of the position measurement. The logic for determining direction is based on the state of the two signals at each edge transition whcih was handled by the interrupt functions.
The current states of A and B were read using digitalRead() and the encoder count was incremented or decremented based on the direction of rotation.
Because interrupts were generated from both encoder channels, the direction condition depended on which channel caused the transition. For an A transition, A != B represented one direction, while for a B transition, the same direction was represented by A == B. Using opposite comparisons for the two channels ensured that all four transitions in a quadrature cycle incremented the count in one physical direction and decremented it in the other. This allowed both encoder channels to improve resolution without their counts canceling each other.

title: Lab 5: Interrupts and Quadrature Encoder
text:
Recoding Pulses and Calculating Velocity
At the end of every 1 second interval, the signed variable encoderCount conatined information on both displacement and direction. A positive value indicated clockwise rotation, while a negative value indicated counter-clockwise rotation. The absolute value of encoderCount was used to calculate the velocity in counts per second.
Once the TIM16 interrupt occurred, the encoderCount was read and reset to zero for the next interval. The velocity and direction were then printed to the terminal.
This specific (25GA-370 DC Motor) was specified as approximately 120 pulses per revolution. Since both edges of both encoder channels were counted, the code defined as 4 times the number of pulses per revolution, or 1632 counts per revolution. The velocity was thus calculated as:
\[
\text{velocity} = \frac{\text{encoder count}}{\text{count / revolution} \times 1\text{s}}
\]
\[
\text{velocity} = \frac{\text{measured Count}}{4*120} \quad (\text{rev/sec})
\]
main.c only performs this calculation whe. measurementReady is set, which occurs in the TIM16 interrupt handler. This ensures that the velocity is only calculated once per second, and that the encoderCount is reset for the next measurement interval.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
In this lab, I built an internet accessible device using the STM32L432KC microcontroller, a DS1722 digital temperature sensor, and an ESP8266 Wi-Fi module. The device hosts a webpage that lets users view the current ambient temperature which updated upon refresh, turn an onboard LED on and off, and choose the resolution of the temperature measurement (shown in ºC) (8, 9, 10, 11, or 12 bits) which controls the decimal places displayed and the accuracy of the measurement.
The MCU was configured to communicate with the DS1722 over SPI using a driver I wrote with the CMSIS register definitions in stm32l432xx.h. The MCU also communicates with the ESP8266 over UART at 125000 baud. When the user loads the webpage or clicks a button, the ESP8266 forwards the request to the MCU, and the MCU reads the sensor, updates the LED or resolution if requested, and sends back a complete HTML page for the ESP8266 to display. This lab demonstrates the use of SPI and UART communication protocols, as well as the integration of a microcontroller with a Wi-Fi module to create an IoT device.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
SPI Driver
The SPI driver was written using the CMSIS register structs and bit definitions from stm32l432xx.h. The initSPI() function first enables the SPI1 peripheral clock and configures PA5, PA6, and PB5 as alternate function 5 so they act as SCK, MISO, and MOSI. It then sets the MCU as the SPI master, sets the baud rate divider, clock polarity, and clock phase based on the temperature sensor specifications from the (datasheet). The FRXTH bit is set to get the flag which is raised as soon as one byte is available, and software slave management is enabled since the chip enable is controlled manually with a GPIO pin. Finally, the peripheral is enabled.
The SPI was initialized with a baud rate setting of 4, which divides the 80 MHz clock by 32 to give a 2.5 MHz SCK, which is below the DS1722’s 5 MHz maximum. CPHA was set to 1 because the DS1722 shifts data out on one clock edge and samples it on the next. The spiSendReceive() function waits until the transmit buffer is empty, writes a byte to the data register, waits until a byte has been received, and returns it. Both the write and the read access the data register so that the hardware performs the necessary 8-bit transfers.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
DS1722 Temperature Sensor Driver
The DS1722 is wired in SPI mode by connecting its SERMODE pin to 3.3V (PIN 7). Its chip enable is active high, so PB4 is driven high at the start of each transaction and low at the end and every exchange consists of an address byte followed by a data byte. Writing to the configuration register uses address 0x80, while the temperature is read from address 0x02 for the most significant byte (MSB) and address 0x01 for the least significant byte (LSB).

Resolution
The resolution is set by writing the sensor’s configuration register, whose bits are 1 1 1 SHOT R2 R1 R0 SD. The setResolution() function keeps SHOT and SD at 0 so the sensor converts continuously, and sets bits R2 through R0 to a value from 0 to 4, which selects 8 to 12 bits of resolution. This gives a configuration byte of 0xE0 | ((bits - 8) << 1), so 8-bit is 0xE0 and 12-bit is 0xE8. Each additional bit halves the temperature step size, from 1 °C at 8-bit down to 0.0625 °C at 12-bit, but also doubles the conversion time, from 75 ms at 8-bit up to 1.2 s at 12-bit. The sensor starts at 9-bit resolution when the program begins as the default resolution.


Temperature Conversion
The readTemperature() function reads the MSB and LSB in two separate transactions. The MSB holds the whole number part of the temperature in two’s complement, and the upper bits of the LSB hold the fractional part, with bit 7 worth 0.5 °C, bit 6 worth 0.25 °C, and so on down to 0.0625 °C. The unused lower bits always read as zero. Combining the two bytes into one 16-bit value gives a number equal to the temperature multiplied by 256, so the temperature is found by:
\[
T = \frac{(\text{MSB} \ll 8) \,|\, \text{LSB}}{256} \quad (^\circ\text{C})
\]
The combined value is cast to a signed 16-bit integer before dividing, which keeps the sign so negative temperatures convert correctly. Since every resolution uses the same bit positions, this single equation works for all five settings and covers the full −10 °C to 30 °C range. For example, a reading of MSB = 0x19 and LSB = 0x10 gives 6416 / 256 = 25.0625 °C, and a reading of MSB = 0xF5 and LSB = 0x80 gives −2688 / 256 = −10.5 °C.
When I first connected the sensor, both bytes read as zero. This was caused by a bug in spiSendReceive(), where the value of the data register was being dereferenced instead of its address. After fixing this, the sensor read room temperature, about 20.5 °C at 9-bit resolution.

title: Lab 6: The Internet of Things and Serial Peripheral Interface
text:
Webpage and Main Loop
The ESP8266 plugs into the mikroBUS socket on the development board, which connects it to USART1 on the MCU. It creates its own Wi-Fi network and hosts the webpage at http://192.168.4.1. When a browser loads the page or a button is clicked, the ESP8266 sends the MCU a request of the form /REQ:<tag>\n, where the tag is the name of the button’s action, such as ledon or res12. The MCU must then send back a complete HTML page, and the ESP8266 forwards it to the browser once it sees </html> or once 200 ms pass without new data.
The main loop handles one request each time it runs. It first reads characters from the UART into a buffer until it receives a newline. It then checks the ledon, ledoff, res8, res9, res10, res11, and res12 tags to see if the user requested a change. If the request is for ledon, it turns on the LED on PB3, if ledoff, it turns off the LED. If the request is for one of the resolution buttons, it writes the new configuration to the DS1722. After any changes, it reads and formats the temperature from the sensor and sends the complete HTML page back to the ESP8266. The page includes the current temperature, the LED status, and buttons for turning the LED on or off and for selecting the resolution. Because the MCU reads the sensor on every request, the temperature updates each time the page is refreshed.
Below are the screenshots of the webpage at 8-bit and 12-bit resolution, showing the temperature in ºC with one and four decimal places, respectively as well as one with the LED on and off.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text: In this lab, I set up the FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array) and MCU (Microcontroller Unit) and tested their functionality. The goal was to design a SystemVerilog-based FPGA system that used four DIP switches as inputs to control three LEDs and a seven-segment display. Combinational logic controlled two of the LEDs according to the specified logic operations and decoded the four-bit switch input for display as a hexadecimal digit on a common-anode seven-segment display. Sequential counter logic, driven by the FPGA’s internal high-speed oscillator (HSOSC), caused the third LED to blink at approximately 2.4 Hz. I simulated the design using QuestaSim before synthesizing and programming it using Lattice Radiant. Finally, I tested the design on the FPGA board to confirm that it functioned as expected.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Development Board Assembly
The provided board 155 board was an empty PCB that was to be popularted with both Through Hpole Technology (THT) and Surface Mount Technology (SMT) components to form the fully assembled board (Figure 1). The various components that I had to solder were the resistors, capacitors, voltage regulator, DIP switches, push-button switches, jumpers, and LEDs. The board also contains the Nucleo-L432KC microcontroller unit (MCU) and the UPduino v3.1 FPGA which were the main components of the board.
Initial testing was done using to ensure that they were workinga nd able to communicate with one another. Lattice Radiant was used to program the FPGA to simply toggle a onboard LED at 1Hz using the HSOSC. The MCU was programmed using Segger Embeeded Studio to blink three other LEDs. After confirming that both the FPGA and MCU were working, I then moved on to designing the SystemVerilog modules.
 Figure 1: My assembled board (left) with the MPU and FPGA, which are powered by the attached microUSB cable or an on-board power supply. Annotated image (right) showing the location ofvarious components of the board.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
FPGA Design and Verilog Structure

Top-Level Module
The SystemVerilog was split into a top-level module and two submodules: one was for the combinational seven-segment display decoder and the other for the sequential counter which controlled led[2] and caused it to blink at 2.4Hz. The overall top module then instantiated both the submodules and the on-board high-speed oscillator (HSOSC) from the iCE40 UltraPlus primitive library. The top module also included the switch-to-led logic to control led[0] and led[1] based on the DIP switch inputs.


Counter Module
Calculations were done to determine the expected number that the counter module would have to go uptil to acheive the desired flashing frequency of 2.4Hz (Period = 1/frequency = 1/2.4Hz = 0.4167s). This period needs account for the rise and fall of the LED, the counter must count for half of this period (0.4167s/2 = 0.2083s). Given the HSOSC frquency of 48MHz, the maxcount was calculated to be 48,000,000 * 0.2083s = 10,000,000. Hence, the counter was designed using the Verilog parameters with maxcount of 10,000,000 and width of 24 bits. After reaching this number, module then resets to zero and toggles led[2], achieving the frequency of 2.4Hz.


Seven-Segment Display Module
The seven-segment display module was designed to decode the four-bit switch input s[3:0] and display the corresponding hexadecimal digit on the common-anode seven-segment display. More specifically, the design of the segment had to account for all numebr 1-9 and letters A-F having a unique display (for exampkle D and 0, thus a lower case d was used). For my module, seg[6] was the most significant bit and responded to A while seg[0] was the least significant bit and responded to G.
The common-anode display meant that the segments were turned on by driving them low, and off by driving them high. The module was designed using case statements with a default case to turn off all segments off when no input or reset is applied.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
Use of Testbenches
Each module was tested individually in QuestaSim using testbenches before hardware testing. These simulated the DIP switch inputs and verified that the outputs (LEDs and seven-segment display) responded correctly according to the design specifications. After testing the submodules, the top-level module was also tested using a testbench to verify that the entire design functioned as expected.

title: Lab 1: FPGA and MCU Setup and Testing
text:
FPGA Hardware Testing Results
After successful simulation of the design, the FPGA was programmed using Lattice Radiant to see if the desired LEDs and seven-segment display turned on as expected. The FPGA board is programmed with the .bin file that is generated after Design Synthesis of the top module. Pins were assigned to the DIP switch inputs s[3:0] and the outputs led[2:0] and seg[6:0] using the Lattice Radiant Pin Assignment tool.
Prior to testing, the seven-segment display HDSP-511C was connected to a breadboard and the pins were connected to the FPGA board using a ribbon cable. The seven segment LEDs were then wired in series with a current-limiting resistor to ensure that the current draw from the FPGA board was less than 200mA and that each diode was getting a current ~8mA. Given that it typically has a forward voltage drop of 2V, and the FPGA board provides 3.3V, the resistor value was calculated as R = (Vdd - Vf)/If = (3.3V - 2V)/0.008A = 162.5Ω. So a standard 160Ω resistor was used.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
In this lab, I explored the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) algorithm and built a hardware implementation on the iCE40 UltraPlus FPGA that performed a 128-bit AES encryption, following the (NIST FIPS-197 specification). The microcontroller was also used to send a 128-bit plain text message and a 128-bit key to the FPGA for encryption over SPI, and the MCU read the 128-bit ciphertext back and checks it against the expected answer from Appendix A.1 and B of the linked standard.
AES scrambles a message over ten rounds. Each round applies four steps to a 4x4 grid of bytes called the state: SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, and AddRoundKey. Additionally there is a separate key expansion process that is used to generate new 128-bit round keys from the original 128-bit key. The full encryption process is very large to build as one block of combinational logic on the FPGA, thus the design helps perform the same AES technique, but only one round at a time and uses the hardware ten different times, with a finite state machine controller helping to sequence the rounds.
The MCU and SPI interface were provided, so the main work for this lab was designing, testing and debugging the aes_core_module on the FPGA and then getting it to work on hardware.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
AES Algorithm Specifications
Before writing the code for this lab, I read through Section 3 to 5.2 of the FIPS 197 specification to understand the details of the AES algorithm, including the structure of the state, the round transformations, and the key expansion process. One detail that mattered throughout the lab is how the state is packed into a 128-bit bus. The bytes fill the 4x4 grid down each column, not across each row, so each 32-bit word of the bus is one column of the state. This means the byte in row r and column c sits at bits [127 - 8(4c + r)] down to 8 bits below that, a formula I used in several modules.
/

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
Datapath Design
The datapath has two 128-bit registers: a state register and a key register. The load signal from the MCU is first synchronized to the FPGA clock by passing it through two flip-flops in series, and only the synchronized version is used inside aes_core. While the synchronized load is high, a mux loads the state register with the plaintext XORed with the key, and a second mux loads the key register with the original key. After loading, each round sends the state register through SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns and AddRoundKey and saves the result back into the state register. At the same time, the key register goes through key expansion and the new round key is saved back into the key register. Both registers are clocked by the system clock and only save when the controller asserts enable.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
SubBytes
The SUbBytes step replaces each of the 16 bytes of the state with a value from the S-box lookup table. I used 16 instances of the provided sbox_sync module, oen per byte. In each instance, one byte of the state feeds into the sbox_sync module and the output is written into the same byte position of the state, since SubBytes only changes the value, not the position. The sbox_sync module is stored in teh FPGA’s embedded blcok RAM rather than logic cells, which is what allows the deisgn to fiton the chip. Given that block RAM is synchronous, the output of the sbox module is available one clock cycle after the input is provided.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
ShiftRows
The ShiftRows step cyclically shifts the bytes in each row of the state to the left by a certain offset. Row 0 is left unchanges, and row 1 is shifted by 1 byte, row 2 by 2 bytes, and row 3 by 3 bytes. This step helps to provide diffusion by mixing the bytes across columns. In hardware this only involved rewiring, and in grid form, the output row r and column c comes from input row r and column (c + r) mod 4 in order to handle the wrap around.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
MixColumns
The MixColumns step takes each column of the state and transforms it using a fixed matrix multiplication in the finite field GF(2^8). This step further mixes the four bytes in each column using Galois field arithmetic, so that every output byte depends on all four input bytes of the column. In hardware, this is typically implemented using combinational logic that performs the necessary finite field multiplications and XOR operations, which was provided to us in the lab. Since the last round of the AES encryption skips MixColumns, I added a bypass mux after this module that selects either the output of MixColumns or output of ShiftRows based on whether it is the last round.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
AddRoundKey
The AddRoundKey was the easiest step to implement, as it simply involves a 128-bit XOR between the current state and the round key.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
Key Expansion
The key expansion module computes the next round key from the current one, following Figure 6 from the FIPS 197 specification shown below. The current key is split into 4 32-bit words, and the last word is put through the three steps of rotation (RotWord) which moves the first byte to the end, S-box substitution of each of the 4 bytes (SubWord) using sbox_sync, and finally XORing with the round constant (Rcon). Since only the top byt of Rcon is ever non-zero, it meant that only the top byte of SubWord result is ever changing.
It involves rotating the last word of the current key, applying the S-box to each byte, XORing with a round constant, and then XORing with the corresponding word of the previous round key to generate the new round key. This process is repeated for each word of the key to produce the complete next round key.
Rcon doubles each round, going from 01 in round 1 to 1B in round 9 and 36 in round 10, and I implemented it as a case statement on the round number. The four new words are then computed as a chain of XORs, where each new word depends on the one just created. Since both key expansion and SubBytes use synchronous S-boxes, the new state and the new round key are ready on the same clock cycle.



Key Expansion

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
Controller FSM
The controler was a separate module I created that contained a four-state FSM and a round counter as shown below. - LOAD: The FSM entered the LOAD state whenever load was high, and the round counter is set to 1. - WAIT: In the WAIT state, the registers hold their values while the S-boxes look up their outputs. This state was necessary because of the one-cycle latency of the synchronous S-boxes. If the registers saved on the first clock edge of a round, they would capture the previous round’s S-box output. Each round therefore takes two clock cycles: one for the S-box lookup and one to save the result. - SAVE: In the SAVE state, the S-box outputs are now valid, so enable is asserted and both registers save the finished round, and the round counter increments. If the round was 10, the FSM moves to DONE, otherwise it returns to WAIT. - DONE: In the DONE state, done is asserted and held, keeping the ciphertext stable until the next load.
The outputs of the controller are the enable signal, the round counter, and the done signal, which indicate when the datapath should save the current round, which round is currently being processed, and when the encryption is complete, respectively.



Controller FSM

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
Top-Level Module
The provided aes module has clk as an input. I wanted to use the iCE40’s internal high-speed oscillator instead of an external clock, thus inside the top-module aes, I instantiated the HSOSC and passed its output to aes as the clock. The HSOSC was configured with CLKHF_DIV = 00, giving a 48MHz clock, similar to what I have used in previous labs.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
SPI Interface
The MCU and FPGA are connected through the SW7 DIP switch on the E155 development board. Using the pin definitions in STM32L432KC_SPI.h and lab7.c together with the board schematic, I assigned the FPGA pins as follows: sck to FPGA pin 21 (MCU PB3), sdi to pin 10 (MCU PB5), sdo to pin 12 (MCU PB4), load to pin 26 (MCU PA5), and done to pin 27 (MCU PA6). PA11 is toggled by the MCU around each byte as an artificial chip-select. It is not used by the FPGA, but it allows the oscilloscope to decode the SPI bytes.

The image below showsn the block diagram for the AES accelerator.The controller FSM helped drive the enable, round and lastround signals while the datapath contains the state and key registrats, SubBytes, ShiftRows, MixColumns, and AddRoundKey modules that were instantiated and connected to form the complete AES round.

text:

The testbench_aes_core testbench applies the FIPS-197 Appendix B key and plaintext to aes_core and checks the ciphertext once done is asserted. The design passed and produced the expected ciphertext 3925841d02dc09fbdc118597196a0b32. Waveform below shows the simulation results for the testbench.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)

Full System Testbench
The testbench_aes_spi testbench shifts the plaintext and key into the full aes module over SPI, waits for done, and shifts the ciphertext back out. The design passed this testbench as well. Waveform below shows the simulation results for the testbench.

title: Lab 7: The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)
text:
Hardware
After programming the FPGA and flashing the MCU, the MCU’s success LED (PA9) lit up, confirming that the FPGA returned the correct ciphertext. However, my first hardware version was unreliable: pressing the MCU reset button sometimes lit the success LED and sometimes lit the failure LED (PA10). Since the pins, SPI and S-boxes were all clearly working on the passing runs, the issue was likely related to timing or reset synchronization between the MCU and FPGA.
After debugging, I found that the cause was the unsynchronized load signal described above. After adding the two-flip-flop synchronizer, the success LED lit on every reset.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display and Keypad Row Scanning
text:
In this lab, I continued the modular FPGA design in Lab 1 by using the combinational seven-segment decoder module which allowed one hexadecimal value to be displayed and the parameterized counter module controlled. This allowed for this lab to focus on integrating a time-multiplexed dual display and a matrix-keypad scanner.
The dual display helped show two independent hexadecimal values using one seven-segment decoder using one shared set of cathode signals. A counter rapidly alternated between the two display digits so that both appeared continuously illuminated.
The keypad scanner sequentially activated four rows with each signal toggling at 2 Hz. Additionally, NPN transistors were used to convert the FPGA row signals into open-collector outputs, while pull-up resistors helped define column logic levels. Red and green LEDs were used to indicate the active row and detected keypad column.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display and Keypad Row Scanning
text:
Hardware Design

Multiplexed Seven-Segment Display
The two common-anode display used one set of seven segment cathode signals that were conmnected in parallel to both digits of the display using the [datasheet] ((https://www.broadcom.com/products/leds-and-displays/7-segment/through-hole/hdsp-5721). The SystemVerilog code implemented a multiplexing counter output which selected one of the two four-bit switch inputs and passed it into the seven-segment decoder. The same counter output enabled the corresponding display digit.
The seven-segment module from Lab 1 was reused without any modifications. The decoder contained combinational logic that translated a 4-bit hexadecimal input into an active-low seven-segment pattern. The multiplexer selection logic added to Lab 2 allowed for this decoder module to be used to take two different 4-bit inputs and serve both displays, displaying the corresponding hexadecimal value independently.
A 2N3906 PNP transistor controlled both the common anode of each digit. These transistors were required because one FPGA output could not safely supply the combined current required when multiple segments were illuminated. Each segment required an individual current-limiting resistor and each PNP base required a resistor to limit current from the FPGA digit enable output.
Ultimately, the display multiplexing frequency needed to be fast enough to present viisble flickering while allowing the electrical signals to settle before the next digit was visible. Given that for human eyesight, a flcikering light blends into a solid image at ~60Hz, I chose a 96Hz (multiple of the high-speed oscillator on the FPGA) as the frequency to flash my digits at.


Keypad Scanner


Figure 1: Image of 4x4 Matrix Keypad Pinout and Circuit Layout. Diagram illustrating the rows and columns terminal assignments alongside the physical membrane keypad layout.

The keypad scanner was the main new module added in Lab 2. It reused an instance of the parameterized counter from Lab 1 and converted the counter state into the four required row patterns.
Each FPGA row outlet drove a 2N3904 NPN transistor configured as an open-collector output. When a row signal was asserted (based on the pre-assigned scanning pattern),the transistor turned on and pulled the corresponding row to low (ground or 0V). Whereas, when the signal was not asserted, the transistor turned off and left the row floating.
The open-collector circuit prevented two FPGA outputs from directly driving against each other when multiple keys were pressed. Each NPN transistor required a resistor between its base and the FPGA output to limit the base current.
Each keypad column was also connected to 3.3V (from the FPGA board) through a pull-up resistor. When no key is pressed, the pull-up resistor helps maintain a defined logic high value. Pressing the key connected the selected row to its correspodning columnm which caused a column to read logic low.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display and Keypad Row Scanning
text:
SystemVerilog Design

Lab 1 Module reuse and parameterization
Lab 2 reused both the counter.sv and sevensegment.sv modules that were tested and verified in Lab 1. The counter module contained the parameters maxcount and width, allowing multiple instances to generate different timing signals without creating separate counter modules, which was incredibly helpful for Lab 2.
One counter was instantiated in the top module to generate the display-multiplexing timing signal. A second counter was instantiated inside the scanning module which was useed to generate the slower keypad-row timing signal which allowed the 4 rows to be scanned twice every second (~2Hz). As mentioned, the seven-segment decoder was also reused and, with Lab 2’s time-multiplexing sleection, allowed for the digits to be driven by different set of inputs.


Multiplexing logic
The multiplexing counter helped perform the two following functions: – It helped select which four-bit hexadecimal input was sent to the seven-segment decoder to be flashed – It enabled the PNP transistor for the matching display digit
The way it worked was that during one interval, the first input was decoded and displayed on the first digit of the dual display. During the next interval, the second input was displayed on the other digit. The process was repeated at a frequency above 60Hz so that, to the humnn eye, both digits appeared continiously illuminated.


Scanning logic
The scanning module contained one parameterized counter and assign statements that used the ternary conditional operator which helped conert the counter output into the four row states to drie the leds and connections between the keypad pins and the FPGA. The module also included an active-low reset and enable input, with reset returning the scanner to its initial row. Disabling the module prevented the counter from advancing, while re-enabling it allowed scanning to continue.


Top-level logic
The top level module contained a internal oscillator, one seven-segment decoder, the multiplexing counter, the scanning module and the assign statemnets for input selection, digit enabling and the scanning passthrough.

title: Lab 2: Multiplexed 7-Segment Display and Keypad Row Scanning
text:
Calculations

Resistor Selection and Current Calculations
Section 4.17 of the iCE40 UltraPlus Family Data Sheet states that an output high current of 8 mA for LVCMOS 3.3 V operation (used for Lab 2). All resistor values calculated below were to ensure that current through each FPGA pin was below 8 mA. The calculations also use the following: – Supply voltage: 3.3V – Red LED forward voltage: 2V – Seven-segment display forward voltage: 2.5V – PNP and NPN silicon base voltage drop: 0.7V
